title: Leading a Table
subtitle: Six sessions that train an ordinary believer to make disciples in a living room, and then to send someone else to do the same
summary: Every table in this library needs someone to set it, and that someone is not a professional. This study trains the disciple maker: why Jesus chose tables and proximity over classrooms and crowds, why hospitality is the actual strategy and not the garnish, how to ask instead of lecture, what to do with silence and with the question you cannot answer, how to care for a person in crisis without pretending to be their counselor, and when and how to send someone out to start a table of their own. Run it as a Sunday school class, a leaders' cohort, or one believer training another across a kitchen table. The goal is not a certificate. It is a room full of people who can each set another table.
setting: A Sunday school room, a living room, a pastor's kitchen. Best done as a group of future table leaders learning together, each already eyeing the table they will set.
forWho: Believers ready to lead others, Sunday school classes training disciple makers, and pastors raising up leaders who multiply.
rhythm: Six sessions, about an hour. Each person should leave session six with names, a place, and a start date.
leaderNote: You are training people to do what you are doing while you do it, so lead this study exactly the way you want them to lead theirs. Ask and wait. Go first in honesty. Admit what you do not know. They will forget most of your sentences and keep most of your habits. And hold the standard loosely but the goal firmly: not everyone will lead the same way, but everyone here is being trained to lead, not to attend. Say that out loud in the first ten minutes of session one.

sessions.title: The Method Was a Table
sessions.bigIdea: Jesus had the crowds and chose the room. He appointed the twelve first of all to be with him, and he was known, to his critics' disgust, for who he ate with. Proximity was the curriculum.
sessions.open: Think of the person who shaped your faith most. How much of what they gave you came through content, and how much through simply being around them?
sessions.read: Read Mark 3:13-15. Jesus appointed twelve so that they might be with him and he might send them out. Notice the order: with him first, sent second. Then read Luke 7:31-35, where Jesus repeats the insult his critics used for him, that the Son of Man has come eating and drinking and they call him a glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners. His reputation was built at tables, and he did not correct it.
observe: In Mark, what are the twelve appointed to before they are given anything to do?
In Luke, what does the accusation against Jesus tell you about how he actually spent his time, and with whom?
talk: The church has often trusted programs, curricula, and stages to make disciples. Jesus trusted shared life at close range. Why do you think we keep reaching for the program, and what does it let us avoid?
You cannot fake proximity. Letting people be with you means they see your ordinary Tuesday, not your prepared self. What about that exposes you, honestly?
If with him comes before sent out, what does that order demand of your own life with Jesus before you set a table for others?
sessions.practice: Audit your week on paper: where do the people you might disciple actually see your unedited life? Choose one recurring point of proximity, a meal, a commute, a standing coffee, and put it on the calendar as the beginning of your table.
sessions.send: You are not building a class. You are opening a life. The table is just where a life gets opened.
sessions.passItOn: Every session of this study ends the same way, with names. Start tonight: write down two or three people you could gather around a table in the next two months.

sessions.title: Hospitality Is the Strategy
sessions.bigIdea: Hospitality is not the decoration around disciple making. It is the delivery system. A guest list that only includes people who can repay you is, by Jesus' definition, the wrong list.
sessions.open: When were you last a guest in someone's actual home, not a restaurant? Why do you think home invitations have become so rare, and what did that one mean to you?
sessions.read: Read Luke 14:12-14. Jesus, himself a dinner guest as he says it, tells his host that when you give a feast, invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, the blind, and you will be blessed, because they cannot repay you. Then read Romans 12:13, where Paul makes it standing policy for every believer: contribute to the needs of the saints and seek to show hospitality. The word Paul uses means love of the stranger, not entertaining friends.
observe: Jesus names the guest lists we default to, friends, relatives, rich neighbors. What is the one thing his replacement list has in common?
Paul says to seek hospitality, to pursue it. What is the difference between hosting when asked and hunting for someone to bring in?
talk: Entertaining says look at my home and performs for guests. Hospitality says you are welcome in my mess and makes room for them. Which one were you raised on, and which one does your home currently practice?
Who cannot repay you in your world right now, socially, financially, spiritually? Put actual faces to the categories in Luke 14. Whose name came to mind first?

What is the honest barrier to your table, the house is too small, the schedule too full, the family too complicated? Say it, then ask the group whether Jesus' own guest list waited for better conditions.
sessions.practice: Before the next session, extend one invitation to someone who cannot repay you and would not expect the invitation. A simple meal. If it is refused, you have still practiced the pursuit, and you will invite again.
sessions.send: The strategy is not clever. It is a door that opens and a pot that stretches. Churches have been planted on less.
sessions.passItOn: Look at your list of names from session one. Ask of each: when were they last inside your home? The answer is your next step.

sessions.title: Ask, Then Stop Talking
sessions.bigIdea: Jesus, who knew every answer, kept asking questions, of lawyers, of blind men, of his own friends. A question honors the person and surfaces the heart. A lecture does neither. The table leader's craft is the question followed by silence.
sessions.open: Recall a time someone asked you a question that stayed with you for days. What made it land deeper than any advice you got that year?
sessions.read: Read Luke 10:25-28. A lawyer stands up to test Jesus with the biggest question there is, and Jesus answers him with two questions: what is written in the Law? How do you read it? The lawyer answers correctly out of his own mouth. Then read Mark 10:51, where Jesus stands in front of Bartimaeus, a blind beggar whose need looks obvious, and still asks, what do you want me to do for you?
observe: In Luke, the expert came to test Jesus and ends up answering his own question. What did Jesus' question do that a lecture could not have done?
In Mark, why might Jesus ask a blind man what he wants? What does the question give Bartimaeus that an unrequested miracle would not?
talk: Why do we lecture? Be honest about the payoff: control, the feeling of competence, the safety of a script. What does the lecturer get to avoid that the asker must endure?

A good table question is open, honest, and answerable by anyone in the room, not a quiz with a right answer hiding in it. Take a question you might ask a group and test it against those three marks. Rework it together.

The hardest discipline is what comes after the question: silence. Count to ten in your head before you rescue the room. Why is it so hard for a leader to let a question hang, and who fills silence fastest in this group?
sessions.practice: In one conversation each day this week, ask a real question and then say nothing until the other person has fully finished, no rescue, no rehearsing your reply while they talk. Report back what the silence produced.
sessions.send: You will be tempted every week to explain. Ask instead. The truth a person says out loud goes deeper than the truth they are told.
sessions.passItOn: Write three open questions for the first session of the table you intend to lead. Read them to this group and let the group test them. Iron sharpens the question.

sessions.title: Silence, and the Question You Cannot Answer
sessions.bigIdea: Job's friends did their best work in the seven days they said nothing, and their worst work the moment they opened their mouths. A table leader must be able to sit in silence and to say the three most trust building words in ministry: I do not know.
sessions.open: Has anyone ever answered your real pain with a quick explanation? What did the fast answer do to your trust in them?
sessions.read: Read Job 2:11-13. Job has lost his children, his wealth, and his health. His three friends come, weep, and then sit with him on the ground seven days and seven nights, and no one spoke a word to him, for they saw that his suffering was very great. The rest of the book is what happened when they finally started explaining, and at the end God says they spoke wrongly. Then read James 1:19. Let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger.
observe: What did the friends do for seven days, and what does the text say they saw that kept them quiet?
James gives three speeds for three actions. Which are we told to be quick at, and which slow?
talk: Someone at your table will one day ask a question you cannot answer, about suffering, about a doctrine, about their own story. What is the fear underneath our need to answer anyway, and what does a fake answer cost the table?
Practice the honest response together, out loud: that is a real question and I do not know. Let me go find out and bring it back next week. Why does that answer build more trust than fluency would?
There is a silence that is empty and a silence that is full, the Job 2 kind, presence without commentary. How can you tell which one a moment needs, and what signals do you watch for?
sessions.practice: Build your bench this week: write down the two or three people you would take a hard question to, your pastor, a wise older believer, a trusted book. A table leader does not need every answer. A table leader needs to know where answers live, and to actually come back with them.
sessions.send: The friends were never asked to explain the whirlwind. They were asked to sit in the ashes. Learn the ashes first.
sessions.passItOn: Tell your group about one question you carried for years before anyone honored it. The leader who remembers being unanswered will never shame an asker.

sessions.title: When Someone at the Table Is in Crisis
sessions.bigIdea: Sooner or later the table will hold a person in real crisis, a collapsing marriage, a diagnosis, a despair that scares you. Your call is to be a shepherd who stays, not a clinician you are not. Presence, prayer, and a walk toward real help.
sessions.open: When your own life cracked, what did the people around you do that actually helped, and what did they do that made it heavier?
sessions.read: Read Psalm 34:17-18. When the righteous cry for help, the LORD hears and delivers them out of all their troubles. The LORD is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit. Then read Galatians 6:2. Bear one another's burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ. Notice what the psalm claims about where God stands in a crisis, near, and what Paul assigns to the church, carrying, not curing.
observe: Where does Psalm 34 locate God when a heart is broken? What does it not promise about the speed of deliverance?
Bearing a burden is different from removing it or explaining it. What does a burden bearer actually do?
talk: The table leader's lane is presence, prayer, Scripture, and follow through. Diagnosis, therapy, and medical judgment belong to people trained and licensed for them. Why is naming your lane an act of love rather than a cop out, and where have you seen well meaning believers wander out of it?

Walk the practical response through together: stay calm, listen without fixing, ask what happened rather than pronouncing what it means, pray with them, and then help them take one concrete step toward the right help, a pastor, a doctor, a licensed counselor. Which of those comes least naturally to you?

Say the safety line out loud as a group until it is second nature: if anyone ever speaks of ending their life, take it seriously every time, stay with them, and get them to real help now. In the United States you can call or text 988, the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, any hour of any day. Whom would you call alongside that, and does your church have a plan you should know tonight?
sessions.practice: Build your referral card this week, on paper or in your phone: your pastor's number, a licensed counselor your church trusts, the 988 line, and one believer who has walked a crisis well. Five minutes of preparation now is love you will be glad you stored.
sessions.send: You are not the rescuer. You are the one who stays in the room and knows the way to help. That is a shepherd's job, and it is enough.
sessions.passItOn: Share your referral card with one other leader in this group and compare notes. Every table in your church should be held by someone who knows the way to help before the night they need it.

sessions.title: When to Send Someone Out
sessions.bigIdea: A table that never sends is a cul-de-sac. Paul's chain in 2 Timothy runs four generations in one sentence, which means the goal of your table was never your table. It was the tables it sets.
sessions.open: Who sent you? Name the person who first trusted you with responsibility in the faith before you felt ready. What did their trust do to you?
sessions.read: Read 2 Timothy 2:1-2. What you have heard from me in the presence of many witnesses entrust to faithful people, who will be able to teach others also. Count the generations in that one verse: Paul, Timothy, faithful people, the others they will teach. Four links. Then read Acts 8:1-4. Persecution scatters the church out of Jerusalem, and those who were scattered went about preaching the word. Not the apostles, verse 1 says they stayed. The ordinary believers carried it.
observe: What is the one qualification Paul names for the people Timothy should entrust the faith to?
In Acts 8, who does the scattering and preaching, and who stayed home in Jerusalem?
talk: How do you know someone is ready to lead a table? Build the list together. Watch for these: they keep showing up, they ask about people by name between sessions, they go first in honesty, they handle Scripture with care even when they handle it simply. What would you add, and notice what is not on the list: polish, credentials, having every answer.

Now the sending itself. The pattern is simple: name it to them plainly, you are ready and I am asking you to set a table. Hand them a study like this one. Sit at their first session or two as a guest, not a boss. Then get out of the way and keep meeting them monthly to hear how it goes. Which step will be hardest for you, and is it hardest because it costs them something or because it costs you your seat?

Some of you feel disqualified from sending because your own table feels unimpressive. Paul wrote this chain from a prison cell. What does the four generation vision do to your definition of a successful table?
sessions.practice: Do the sending math this week. Write the names of everyone at your current or planned table and mark the one or two who show the readiness signs. Pray for them daily. Then set a date within the month to have the sending conversation with one of them.
sessions.send: Your table was never the destination. It was the seedbed. Send, and the thing outlives you.
sessions.passItOn: This study is free, and it was built to be handed on. Give a copy of it to the person you are sending, take them through session one as their guest, and let the chain add its next link.
